records.table: Hennessy Very Special, the V.S on the label, is the young cognac of the house an Irish officer founded in Cognac in 1765, blended from some forty eaux-de-vie of four crus. Toast, almond and brown sugar carry it neat, long with ginger ale or in a French 75.
records.story: Richard Hennessy (1724 to 1800), born in County Cork, served the French king in the Irish Brigade, then settled in Cognac and founded a trading house for its eaux-de-vie in 1765. In the early 1800s the house took on a cooper of the Fillioux family as its blender, by its own account, and his sons and grandsons followed him into the role for generations. By the house's account every eau-de-vie it uses is tasted by its committee before it goes into a blend. In 1865, by the house's own account, the family helped bring in grading by stars, and the Three Star cognac of that system is the line that the V.S of the label carries on. In 1971 Hennessy merged with the Champagne house Moët et Chandon to form Moët Hennessy, and in 1987 Moët Hennessy merged with Louis Vuitton to form LVMH. The V.S earns its place behind the bar as the house's young cognac, poured long or in a Sidecar, and as the bottle on which to explain what grade letters promise: a floor of two years in oak, not an age.

records.story: In 1724 a vine grower born near Rouillac set up a cognac trading house under his own name, by the house's account, and the business stayed with his family for generations. In 1924 André Renaud (died 1965) took charge of the house and became, by its account, its first cellar master. In 1927 he launched the VSOP Fine Champagne, a blend drawn only from the two chalky crus at the heart of the region, and in 1938 the Fine Champagne name was set down in the law of the appellation. When Renaud died in 1965, his son-in-law took over the firm. In 1990 the holding companies of Rémy Martin and of Cointreau, the orange liqueur house of Angers, merged, and in 1991 the group took the name Rémy Cointreau. The house kept its rule of blending from the two Champagne crus alone. Two label words are learnt from this one bottle: VSOP, a promise about age, and Fine Champagne, a promise about origin that has nothing to do with sparkling wine.

records.story: Born at St Brelade in Jersey, Jean Martell (1694 to 1753) set up as a merchant of eaux-de-vie in Cognac, on the Charente, in 1715. His descendants built a house style on the Borderies, a small cru whose eaux-de-vie are round and floral, and on clear wine distilled without its lees. In 1912 the founder's great-grandson created Cordon Bleu, an extra old cognac given a name of its own; by the house's account it was launched at the Hôtel de Paris in Monaco. The blend, of more than a hundred eaux-de-vie, has kept its name since. The family ran the firm for most of three centuries. Seagram, which had bought a large share in 1987, took full control of the house in 1988, and Pernod Ricard acquired it with Seagram's drinks business in 2001. Ask what a cru brings to a blend, and Cordon Bleu, built on the Borderies, is the answer to pour, set beside the house's arched XO decanter.

records.table: At Jarnac on the Charente, Courvoisier VSOP is blended from four crus, Fins Bois among them, and aged up to twelve years in the house's own oak. Stone fruit, toasted almond and gingerbread hold their own in a Sidecar.
records.story: Courvoisier counts its years from 1828. By the house's account a Paris wine and spirits firm at Bercy, run by the founder's father and a partner, passed to their sons, who set up a new business at Jarnac on the Charente that dealt in cognac alone. The brand's legend reaches further back: the story goes that the emperor Napoléon Bonaparte (1769 to 1821) visited the Bercy cellars in 1811, and the brand has long told itself as the cognac of Napoléon. The founding son left no heir, and the house passed to his nephews, who in 1869, by the house's account, were named suppliers to the court of Napoléon III (1808 to 1873). In 1909 the Simon family, the house's distributors in Britain, took over the firm and, by one account, gave it the slogan the Brandy of Napoléon. The house changed hands several times in the century that followed, and in 2024 Campari bought it from Beam Suntory. Four crus, a round, fruity middle and enough body to carry citrus in a Sidecar: the VSOP is the working cognac of the house.

records.table: Ferrand 1840 Original Formula answers the old recipes: a Grande Champagne cognac blended after a bottle of 1840 made for mixing, and bottled at 45 per cent so its fruit outlasts ice and sugar. Ripe grape, honey and spice stand up in a julep or a Brandy Crusta.
records.story: The Ferrand name comes from a family of growers at Ségonzac, in Grande Champagne, where, as the house tells it, ten generations of its men, each named Elie, worked the vines and stills over three centuries. By the house's account the family built its manor there in 1861, and the line of Elies ended in 1915, when an Elie serving in the First World War died of typhoid. In 1989 a new firm, Maison Ferrand, was founded to revive the name, and by its account the Château de Bonbonnet at Ars became the heart of its work. In 2011 the house released 1840 Original Formula, made with its cellar master and a drinks historian to recreate the three star cognac that bartenders of the nineteenth century poured into punches, juleps and crustas. The blend was modelled closely on a well-kept bottle of Pinet-Castillon cognac from 1840, and it is bottled at 45 per cent, above the 40 of most young cognacs, so that it keeps its fruit once it meets ice and sugar. Its purpose is the old recipes, made as their authors wrote them: reach for it when a guest asks for a julep, a crusta or a punch.
